subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Dunning-Kruger Effect
description: A quick win: understand The Dunning-Kruger Effect.

hook.text: A bank robber covered his face in lemon juice, believing it made him invisible to cameras.

buildup.text: Dunning and Kruger found that the least skilled people overestimate their ability the most.

discovery.text: Low competence prevents recognizing low competence. You need skill to know you lack it.

twist.text: Experts do the opposite: they underestimate themselves because they see how much they still don't know.

climax.text: Confidence peaks at the start and at mastery. The painful middle is where real learning happens.

punchline.text: Doubt is a sign you're getting smarter.

quiz.question: Why do the least skilled overestimate their abilities?
options: They lack the skill needed to recognize their incompetence
They have had too much training

details.summary: The Dunning-Kruger effect describes how people with limited knowledge in a domain overestimate their competence while genuine experts tend to underestimate theirs. Incompetence prevents people from recognizing their own incompetence, creating confident ignorance.
details.whyItMatters: The Dunning-Kruger effect explains why overconfident beginners dominate discussions while cautious experts hold back. In organizations, it means the most vocal contributors may be the least competent, while true expertise stays quiet.
takeaways: Low-skill individuals systematically overestimate their own competence
High-skill individuals tend to underestimate their relative expertise
Gaining competence improves self-assessment by revealing what you do not know

faq.question: Why do beginners think they know more than they do?
faq.answer: They lack the very knowledge needed to evaluate their own knowledge. Without understanding the full scope of a field, they cannot see how much they are missing. It takes expertise to recognize the boundaries of expertise.

faq.question: Why do experts underestimate their own abilities?
faq.answer: Experts can see the vast landscape of what they still do not know. They also assume that what they know is common knowledge, underestimating how much their expertise exceeds the average. This is sometimes called the curse of knowledge.
